glance: 140 km to Lakshmipur by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
alexander-meghna-beach.desc: Near Alexander, the Ramgati upazila headquarters, the embankment along the Meghna has become a popular riverside beach. The river here is enormous, with boats and fishing nets dotting the water and the far bank barely visible. In the evenings families gather for snacks and the sunset over the water.
blocks: How to get there
About 1.5 hours by bus or CNG south from Lakshmipur town to Alexander, Ramgati.
Good to know
Keep children well back from the bank; the river is strong and banks can erode. Avoid swimming.

khoa-sagar-dighi.desc: Khoa Sagar Dighi is a very large old tank near Dalal Bazar, one of the biggest in the district. Local stories connect it with the old landlords of the area. It sees few visitors from outside, and its banks are a peaceful place to sit by the water, especially in the soft light of winter afternoons.
blocks: How to get there
Near Dalal Bazar; combine with the zamindar bari. Ask locals for directions.
Good to know
There are few facilities; carry water.

glance: 140 km to Lakshmipur by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
dalal-bazar-zamindar-bari.desc: This former zamindar's estate in Dalal Bazar once spread across a large compound of palaces, temples and ponds. The family left in the turmoil of the 1940s, and many buildings fell into ruin, with trees growing from their walls. The Department of Archaeology has restored part of the complex and set up a museum there. Walking among the arches and the old pond gives a sense of the area's past wealth.
blocks: How to get there
About 20 minutes by CNG from Lakshmipur town toward Dalal Bazar.
Good to know
Be careful around unstable ruined walls. Check museum days locally.

lakshmipur-buffalo-curd-feast.desc: In Lakshmipur, the last course of a wedding or community feast is buffalo-milk curd, served in generous portions from clay pots. Locals see it as a matter of honour; serving curd made from cow's milk instead can be taken as a slight to the guests. The custom keeps a whole chain of herders and curd-makers on the chars in business.

glance: 140 km to Lakshmipur by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
majhu-chowdhury-hat.desc: Majhu Chowdhury Hat is a market and river port in Char Ramani Mohan union of Lakshmipur Sadar, founded in 1965 at a place once called Rahmatkhali. Launches, trawlers and ferries cross the Meghna from here to Bhola, so the ghat is always busy with passengers, fishing boats and stalls. In the afternoon people come simply to sit on the embankment and watch the wide river and the sunset.
blocks: How to get there
From Lakshmipur town take a CNG or bus to Majhu Chowdhury Hat (about 30–40 minutes).
Good to know
In the monsoon the Meghna can be rough; check weather signals before boarding any boat. Go in the late afternoon for the sunset.

glance: Markets in Ramgati, Kamalnagar and Lakshmipur town
ramgati-mohisher-doi.desc: Herds of buffalo graze on the river islands off Ramgati and Kamalnagar, and their milk is set into dense, sour curd in clay pots. Ramgati's curd is especially well known. It is eaten after big meals, with flattened rice and molasses, or on its own, and is produced in large quantities for weddings and feasts.

glance: 140 km to Lakshmipur by road, 4–5 hours by bus or car
raipur-jinn-mosque.desc: This mosque, built in the late 19th century about a kilometre from Raipur town, is known locally as the Jinn Mosque because of stories that it was raised overnight by supernatural beings. The legend is what made it famous, but the building's domes and decoration are also a good example of the local style of the period.
blocks: How to get there
From Lakshmipur town take a bus or CNG to Raipur (about 40 minutes), then a rickshaw.
Good to know
Avoid prayer times and dress modestly.

glance: Daab sellers and bazars in Lakshmipur town and across Sadar upazila
lakshmipur-coconut.desc: Coconut palms grow around almost every house in Lakshmipur, and the district produces crores of dried coconuts a year, mostly from Sadar upazila. Locals drink green daab in the heat and use grated coconut in pithas, naru and curries. The husks feed a busy coir trade, so you will see coconut in every bazar here.

glance: Riverside fish ghats such as Majuchowdhurir Hat, Motirhat, Khaser Hat (Raipur) and Char Alexander (Ramgati)
lakshmipur-meghna-ilish.desc: Lakshmipur's western edge is the wide Meghna, and about 30 fish ghats line the river from Raipur down to Char Alexander and Ramgati. In season boats land hilsa all day, and many of the fish sold in Chandpur's markets actually come from these waters. Buying at a ghat like Motirhat or Majuchowdhurir Hat, you can have it fried or cooked in mustard at a nearby hotel.

glance: Wholesale haats in Lakshmipur town and Raipur
lakshmipur-supari.desc: Villages across Lakshmipur are shaded by slim areca palms, and supari is a major cash crop for local families. After harvest, nuts are dried in the sun or soaked in water and sold through busy wholesale markets. Chewed with betel leaf, it is part of hospitality across Bangladesh. Coconut palms grow alongside, and fresh green coconuts are sold on every roadside.
